title: Far From Home
subtitle: Luebeck. 28 days. 20 euros.

shape.rule: Introduce mechanics on the widening half. Master them on the narrowing half.

acts.name: One thread
acts.intent: Arrival, one conversation, and the der/die/das ramp. Ends on the Aha.

acts.name: Two threads
acts.intent: The Kaution fork: pay it and be broke, or borrow and keep a runway.

acts.name: Four to six threads
acts.intent: Every remaining system arrives here. Peak chaos.

acts.name: Threads close
acts.intent: Nothing new is introduced. Mastery and untangling only.

prose: So this is Germany. Clean. Tidy. And possessing a bus shelter roughly the size of a toaster. If I try to stand under that, my knees will stick out into oncoming traffic.
Twenty euros in my jacket pocket. A visa that expires in four weeks. And a handwritten note with 'Room 4, WG Am Burgtor' on it.

choices.label: Take the canal path (Scenic walk along the ironed river)
Take the cobblestone alley (Direct, but watch your ankles)

scenes.beat: arrival / hope + first cold

prose: You walk by the canal. The river is so flat it looks like someone ironed it with heavy starch.
On a stone bench sits an empty bottle with a tiny recycling mark. In England this is rubbish; here it pays 25 cents! (+€0.25 Pfand)
You drag your 25kg suitcase over medieval cobblestones. Nature's way of punishing human ankles.
Room 4 is on the second floor of a stepped-gable Altbau. The stairwell smells of old floor wax and radiators.
Outside the kitchen, a tall lad in woolen socks is standing frozen over the counter with a mug of peppermint tea.
Nico: Halt! Don't move! Are you the new flatmate for Room 4?
You: Yeah, mate. Just dragged my suitcase across the bridge.
Nico: Put the bag down slowly. We have to address something of international diplomatic importance.

choices.label: "Is everything alright? Did I step on a historic brick?"
prose: Nico: Worse. Much worse. Come into the kitchen.

choices.label: "I've been travelling two days. Can this wait five minutes?"
prose: Nico: German municipal waste regulations wait for no man. Five minutes is enough for Herr Becker to issue a 25-euro fine.

scenes.beat: first kindness / the mug

prose: Nico points dramatically at the three plastic bins beneath the sink.
Nico: Two things before you unpack.
Nico: One - the university office shuts at 17:00 sharp. It's now past six. If you knock at 17:01, they look at you like you've committed treason.
Nico: Two - and I am genuinely begging you here. Mülltrennung. The bins.

choices.label: "The bins. Right. What's the exam?"
prose: Nico: Blue is paper, yellow is plastic and foil, black is everything else.
Nico: Herr Becker patrols with a flashlight. If he finds a yogurt lid in the blue bin, our clothes will be on the pavement by midnight.

choices.label: "It's rubbish, mate. Does it really matter?"
prose: Nico recoils in sheer horror and covers his coffee mug.
Nico: Does it matter?! In Germany, recycling is not a hobby, it is a spiritual test!

scenes.beat: setup: office shut + the bins

choices.label: "Blue paper, yellow plastic/foil, black rest. Got it, chief."
prose: Nico lets out a long, trembling sigh of relief.
Nico: Brilliant. You're a legend. Here, have some peppermint tea.

choices.label: "Twenty-five euros for a misplaced banana peel?!"
prose: Nico grins weakly.
Nico: Wait until you meet the Bürgeramt.

scenes.beat: PLANT: pays off day 11 as a 25 euro fine

prose: Nico taps an official-looking brown envelope on the kitchen desk.
Nico: One more crisis. That letter arrived for Room 4 this afternoon.
You open it: Hochschule Lübeck — 250€ Semesterbeitrag matriculation due by Friday, or your visa registration is cancelled.
Nico: You have twenty quid and four weeks on your visa. You need cash tonight. Head toward the Holstentor market — there's always someone hiring if you have legs.

choices.label: "Two hundred and fifty euros?! I need to run to the Uni right now!"
prose: Nico: Go on then, but don't say I didn't warn you about German office hours.

choices.label: "Market by the Holstentor. Understood. I'll check the campus first."
prose: Nico: Good luck. Watch out for Frau Meier on the ground floor — don't slam the door!

scenes.beat: MOTIVATES finding work tonight — player must discover Kruma Express themselves via pizzeria and bakery

prose: You sprint across the cobbled canal bridge to the Admissions Hall.
The enormous oak double doors are chained shut with a padlock the size of a teacup saucer.
A laminated sign reads: 'Öffnungszeiten: Di & Do 10:00 - 11:30. Freitags geschlossen.'
You mutter: 'Ninety minutes a week?! What do they do the rest of the time, polish their rubber stamps?!'

choices.label: "Can I just knock? It's barely past five!"
prose: Frau Klein (passing by with canvas bags of potatoes): Haha! Liebling, at 16:59:59 the pen leaves the hand. At 17:01 the secretary is on her sofa drinking chamomile tea.
Frau Klein: If you bang on that door now, the police will arrive with a decibel meter. Try the market for work, lad.

choices.label: "Ninety minutes a week. Of course. Why would anyone expect otherwise?"
prose: Frau Klein chuckles dryly from the steps: Exactly, young man. Welcome to Germany! Now off to the pizzeria if you need bread.

scenes.beat: first defeat / the locked door — player now searches for work: pizzeria then bakery then Kruma

prose: The pizzeria shutter is half raised. A cloud of hot garlic, oregano, and boiling anger drifts into the street.
Mathias Becker is aggressively slamming a ball of dough against a marble counter.
You: Good evening! Any chance you're hiring a delivery courier?
Mathias stops, wipes flour on his apron, and looks you up and down like you're an uninvited tax auditor.
Mathias: Delivery driver?! Do you speak Italian? No! Do you know how to spin dough? No! And your German sounds like a broken lawnmower!
Mathias: We are closed! Try the bakery down the street before I throw this rolling pin!

choices.label: "Right. Charming. Have a lovely evening, mate."
prose: You back out slowly. The garlic smell lingers on your jacket for two blocks.

choices.label: "Can I leave my number just in case?"
prose: Mathias points menacingly with a wooden pizza peel toward the street exit.
You decide walking is the better option.

scenes.beat: REJECTION 1: pizzeria — too late, no one to train, try elsewhere

prose: A warm amber glow shines through the glass of Bäckerei Hansa. An elderly baker in a white apron is dusting flour off a wooden peel.
You knock gently on the door. She looks at the clock, shakes her head, but turns the brass key anyway.
Martha Beck: We are closed, my dear. Unless you want a loaf of day-old Roggenbrot?
You: Actually, Frau Beck, I'm looking for work. Anything honest.
Martha Beck: To knead bread in Germany you need a B1 language certificate and three years of flour apprenticeship! My customers want to chat about the Baltic weather in proper German.
She softens, looks at your thin jacket, and slips a warm Franzbrötchen pastry into your hand.
Martha Beck: But listen to me. Around the corner near the Holstentor is Kruma Express. A dark store. Night delivery couriers. They sort by ear, not with certificates.
Martha Beck: Nina Voss manages dispatch. Tell her Martha sent you. And eat that pastry before it gets cold!

choices.label: "Kruma Express. Thank you so much, Frau Beck!"
prose: You eat the Franzbrötchen while walking. Cinnamon, butter, sugar. Genuinely the best thing you've eaten since landing in Hamburg.

choices.label: [Bow gratefully, take the pastry, and march toward Kruma.]
prose: Warm cinnamon pastry in hand, you pick up the pace toward the neon green glow of the warehouse.

scenes.beat: REJECTION 2 / DISCOVERY: bakery — language barrier, but Martha gives the Kruma lead and a Franzbroetchen
scenes.sets_note: first meeting with Martha — she remembers this

prose: The Kruma Express warehouse is humming with conveyor belts and industrial chillers.
Nina Voss stands by the dispatch desk, clipboard in one hand, double espresso in the other.
Nina Voss: You're the temp Martha mentioned. Good. Shift starts now.

Nina Voss: Listen carefully: warehouse shelves are sorted by German grammar gender. Bottom shelf is DER (Blue ▲). Middle shelf is DIE (Pink ●). Top shelf is DAS (Purple ■). Learn the word and you cut your search time by two thirds!

choices.label: [Clock in: Audio + icon arrive together. Pure muscle memory.]
prose: "Die Milch!" Pink shelf glows. "Der Apfel!" Blue shelf glows. "Das Brot!" Purple shelf glows.
Nina Voss: Exactly! Keep that pace and you might actually survive the week.

scenes.beat: TEACH: audio and icon together, cannot fail. Mechanic introduced.

prose: Second manifest. The warehouse bell rings louder.
The audio voice calls out 1.5 seconds BEFORE the shelf lights up! Guessing by shelf color tier earns a 2.0x Early Pick Bonus!
Nina Voss: Pick on the sound, rookie! Don't wait for your eyes!

choices.label: [Listen for the article and pick before the shelf glows!]
prose: You hear 'Der Kaffee' and slam the bottom blue shelf before the icon even renders. Double early payout!

scenes.beat: ANTICIPATE: 1.5s icon delay. Player starts listening, not looking.

prose: Shift 3. Pure audio recognition. The visual helper icons are gone completely.
The voice calls: 'Die Banane!' Your hand instinctively darts to the middle shelf.
You've been in Germany for barely three hours, and you're sorting municipal logistics by German grammatical gender in under 0.1 seconds.

choices.label: [Finish the rush order by ear!]
prose: Nina Voss checks the dispatch terminal with a faint smirk.
Nina Voss: Not bad, England. Not bad at all. Print the receipt.

scenes.beat: THE AHA. Icon never arrives; the grammar has become spatial instinct.

payout.formula: base 15.0 + perfect audio accuracy + customer doorstep tip

prose: The register chimes as an itemized payslip prints out.
Nina Voss: Base wage 15€, accuracy bonus, 2.0x early streak, and a polite customer tip for saying Bitte at the door.
Nina Voss: That's 52.50€ earned across your first three runs. Reinvest in the Bike Shop for an E-Bike, or save it for your 250€ tuition.

choices.label: [Fold the receipt into your passport.]
prose: Fifty-two quid in one evening. Still a long way to 250€, but your tuition bar is visibly climbing.

scenes.beat: THE RECEIPT: names the money so the tuition bar means something
scenes.econ_note: no wallet change here: the three shift scenes already paid 9.50 + 10.50 + 11.50 = 31.50

prose: You have {wallet}€.
Two hundred and fifty is not a number you can look at directly yet. It is more like weather.
scenes.beat: the number 250 lands as weather

prose: The canal is completely still. The lanterns lie down flat on it, orange and unbroken, and you stand there longer than you meant to.
Your phone buzzes. Home. They will have been waiting up.

choices.label: "It's beautiful here. Everything's fine. The room's great."
prose: You hear your mother let a breath out. It is worth the lie. That is the thing about this particular lie - it is genuinely worth it.

choices.label: "I got in late. I missed the office. I have seventeen euros."
prose: Silence on the line. Then your father, who never takes the phone, takes the phone.
"So you'll go at nine tomorrow," he says. "That's all this is. You'll go at nine."
It fixes nothing. You sleep better anyway.

scenes.beat: THEME: the worthwhile lie / mirrored in four_phone

prose: Room 4 has a bed, a desk, a window, and a radiator that ticks.
You do not unpack. You will not unpack for eleven days.
scenes.beat: the suitcase stays packed for 11 days

prose: There is a man in the stairwell holding a clipboard like a weapon.
Herr Hans Lokker: Room 4. You arrived last night at eighteen forty.

choices.label: "You were counting?"
prose: Herr Hans Lokker: I was awake.

choices.label: "Good morning."
prose: A nod. Very small.
Herr Hans Lokker: Morgen.

scenes.beat: the antagonist who is not one

prose: Herr Hans Lokker: Kaution. Deposit. Thirty euros. You have three days.
Herr Hans Lokker: No deposit, no signed lease. And you will find that without a signed lease this city does not believe you live in it.
He is not enjoying this. Somehow that is worse than if he were.

choices.label: "I have {wallet}€."
prose: Herr Hans Lokker: Then you have a problem, and three days in which to have had it.
At the stairs, without turning: Kruma Express. Behind the Holstentor. They are always short of somebody.

choices.label: "You'll have it."
prose: Herr Hans Lokker: Good. I prefer that answer. It is usually not true, but I prefer it.

scenes.beat: INCITING: 30 euros in 3 days

prose: You have thirty-one fifty in your pocket and Lokker wants thirty of it.
Which is fine. Which is exactly fine, and leaves you one euro fifty and a two hundred and fifty euro tuition bill.
Two streets over there is a pizzeria with the shutter half up, and a man inside with a bicycle upside down on a table.

choices.label: [Pay Lokker the thirty. Be broke and owe nobody.]
prose: You count it twice on the stairs before you knock, which does not change the number.

choices.label: [Try the pizzeria first. Keep the thirty-one fifty as a runway.]
prose: The shutter is half up. You duck under it, which feels like the wrong way to enter a business.

scenes.beat: THE FORK, REFRAMED: pay it and be broke, or borrow and keep a runway

prose: Lokker counts it twice, then writes on a form in handwriting from another century.
Herr Hans Lokker: Wohnungsgeberbestaetigung. Landlord's confirmation. This proves you sleep here.
Herr Hans Lokker: Take it to the Buergeramt. They will not believe you exist without it, and I am not being funny.
Wallet: {wallet}€.

choices.label: "Thank you, Herr Lokker."
prose: He is already inspecting the bins.
Herr Hans Lokker: Blue is paper.

scenes.beat: FIRST PAPER WON / both threads converge here

prose: One piece of paper. It weighs nothing. You keep checking that it is still in your pocket.
Nico is in the kitchen with three books open and none of them being read.
Nico: You got the lease? On day two?
He puts a hand up for a high five, converts it to a handshake halfway, and the result is a mess.
Nico: Okay. Don't get comfortable. Tomorrow it stops being one thing at a time.
scenes.beat: the botched high five / warning: it stops being one thing at a time

prose: You wake up knowing four things at the same time, which is one more than a person can hold.
Two hundred and fifty euros, before the visa appointment on the twenty-eighth.
A stamp at the Buergeramt.
A bank account.
And rent, eight euros, every single morning, whether or not you got out of bed.
scenes.beat: CHAOS OPENS: four problems held at once

prose: Marktplatz. Cobbles. A tram bell somewhere. {day > 12:The days have started to look the same, which is its own kind of danger.}

Day {day} of 28. Wallet {wallet}€. Body {body}. { has_lease:Lease: yes.|Lease: no.} { has_anmeldung:Anmeldung: stamped.|Anmeldung: not stamped.} { has_konto:Account: open.|Account: frozen.} { matriculated:Matriculated.|Tuition still owed.}

choices.label: The yard behind Kruma. Klaus is out there again.
The WG kitchen. Nico hasn't slept.
The shop counter at Kruma. Spend money to make money.
Bakery Hansa. It's warm in there.
The AStA office. Somebody said there's a lawyer.

scenes.beat: PLAYER AGENCY: work the knots in any order

prose: Herr Vogel has a desk, a stamp, and a queue, and he loves exactly one of those things.
Herr Vogel: Anmeldung. Passport. Landlord's confirmation. Bank details.

choices.label: Hand over the passport and the lease.
prose: He reads both. Slowly. Then looks up with an expression of real regret, which you were not expecting.
Herr Vogel: And your German bank account.

scenes.beat: KNOT 1 opens
the deadlock is named

prose: You go to the Sparkasse. It takes eleven minutes to walk and four minutes to understand.
Frau Weber: I can open the account the moment you bring me your Meldebescheinigung. Your registration certificate.

choices.label: "From the Buergeramt."
prose: Frau Weber: From the Buergeramt.

choices.label: "The man at the Buergeramt wants the bank account first."
prose: Frau Weber, without any change of expression at all: Yes.

scenes.beat: the other half of the circle

prose: You stand on the pavement between the two buildings, which are four hundred metres apart, and you do the loop again in your head to check.
The Buergeramt needs the bank. The bank needs the Buergeramt. The university needs both. The visa needs the university.
Nothing in this circle is anybody's fault. That is the part that gets to you. There is nobody to be angry at. It is just a shape, and you are inside it.

choices.label: Sit down on the step for a minute.
prose: You sit down on the step of a bank in a country where you know six people, and for about ninety seconds you are not okay.
Then you get up, because the alternative is to keep sitting there.

choices.label: Go and find somebody who has seen this before.
prose: Somebody has seen this before. Somebody has to have seen this before. Four hundred metres apart, for decades - somebody knows the way through.

scenes.beat: EMOTIONAL LOW / nobody to be angry at

prose: The bicycle on the table has no back wheel. The man has one hand inside the frame and flour on his forearm.
Herr Mathias Becker: We open at eleven. Unless you're here about the bike, in which case sit down.

choices.label: "I'm here about thirty euros."
prose: He stops. Wipes his hands. Looks at you properly, which nobody has done since you arrived.
Herr Mathias Becker: Ah. Kaution. Lokker.

choices.label: "What's wrong with the bike?"
prose: Herr Mathias Becker: Everything. It's forty years old and I am not throwing it out.
You hold the frame while he seats the wheel. It takes eleven minutes. He talks the whole time and none of it is about you, which is a relief.
Herr Mathias Becker: Now. What did you actually come in here for.

scenes.beat: THEME: the debt you repay forward, not back

prose: Herr Mathias Becker: Naples. Nineteen ninety-four. I arrived with a bag and a cousin's address, and the cousin had moved.
He says it flatly, like a weather report.
Herr Mathias Becker: Somebody gave me forty marks. I never paid him back, because he wouldn't let me. So.
He puts three tens on the table and slides them across with two fingers.
Herr Mathias Becker: Thirty. You pay me back when it's easy, not when it's hard. And if you come in here looking guilty I will throw a pizza at you.

choices.label: "I'll pay you back."
prose: Herr Mathias Becker: Yes, yes. Go. Lokker's awake. Lokker is always awake.

choices.label: "I can't take this. I don't know you."
prose: He pushes it two centimetres further.
Herr Mathias Becker: That is the correct answer and it is also stupid. Take the money.

scenes.beat: Naples 1994 / the debt you repay forward, not back

prose: Nina Voss: Shift {shift_no}. Manifest's longer than yesterday. It gets longer every day, that's not a mistake, that's the job growing.

prose.text: The voice in the ceiling comes a beat before the icon now. You notice it, and you start picking on the word instead of the picture.
Today the icon does not come at all until you are already holding the thing. You have stopped looking at the shelves. You are listening.
Your back has a new opinion about the bottom shelf. Der Kaese is down there. Der Kaese is always down there.

prose: ~ temp pay = 10.0 + 3.0 * shift_no + 12.5
Payout: {pay}€. Wallet: {wallet}€. Body: {body}.

prose.text: The e-bike does the hill on Grosse Petersgrube for you. You had forgotten there was a hill.

choices.label: "Nina. Can I ask you something that isn't about work."

scenes.beat: KNOT 2 / the audio ramp TEACH->ANTICIPATE->TEST

prose: Nina Voss: You can ask. I might not answer.

choices.label: "The Auslaenderbehoerde. The director there is called Lindemann."

scenes.beat: RELATIONSHIP AS CURRENCY: sets up act_five reference

prose: She puts the tablet down, which she has never once done.
Nina Voss: She's my sister.

choices.label: "...Oh."
prose: Nina Voss: We don't speak. Eleven years. It's not interesting, it's just old.

choices.label: "Does that help me or hurt me?"
prose: One short laugh again.
Nina Voss: Straight to the point. Good.

scenes.beat: reveal: Nina and Dr Lindemann are sisters

prose: Nina Voss: It does nothing for you. She'd throw out anything with my name on it and she'd be right to.
Nina Voss: But I'll tell you what does work on her. She reads the file. The whole file. Every page, every time. She's the only one left in that building who does.
Nina Voss: So make the file good. Not sad. Good.
scenes.beat: the actionable advice: make the file good, not sad

prose: A laminated sheet by the clock-out terminal. Company gear, staff price, deducted or cash.
Wallet: {wallet}€.

choices.label: E-Bike. 45€. The hills stop existing.
prose: Klaus, from the yard, without looking up: Best money you'll ever spend. Ask my knees.

choices.label: Thermal Bag. 50€. Things arrive cold that should be cold.
prose: Nina Voss: Tips go up. People tip freshness, they just think they're tipping you.

choices.label: Vocab Cards. 35€. Der, die, das, on paper, in your pocket.
prose: You learn eleven words on the tram. Tomorrow you will pick eleven things before the icon shows up, at double.

choices.label: Shelf Labels. 25€. Your handwriting, on the racks.
prose: You label the rows yourself, in marker, in your own hand. It is the first thing you have changed here.

choices.label: Pocket Notepad. 20€. For the things people tell you once.
prose: Blue paper. Yellow plastic. Black rest. Nine o'clock, notes not coins. You write it all down.

choices.label: Leave it. Every euro in the tin is a euro toward the two-fifty.

prose.text: You do the arithmetic and the arithmetic says no. Not yet.|Buying something feels like going backwards. It isn't. But it feels like it.

scenes.beat: INVEST / HARVEST / UPGRADE spine
scenes.sets_note: has_ebike, has_thermalbag, has_vocabcards, has_labels, has_notepad, knows_trennung

prose: Klaus is sitting on an upturned crate with one leg straight out in front of him, wrapping his knee in a bandage he has clearly wrapped a thousand times.
Klaus der Blitz: Fourteen years. They called me the lightning. Now I get called by the physio.

choices.label: "Fourteen years?"
prose: Klaus der Blitz: Fourteen. I was going to do two.
Klaus der Blitz: That's how it gets you. Not all at once. Two more years, fourteen times.

choices.label: "Does it get better?"
prose: Klaus der Blitz: The knee? No. The job? Also no. You get better. That's the only variable.

scenes.beat: KNOT 3 / THE MIRROR: 14 years, meant to do 2

prose: Klaus is still on the crate. He is always on the crate now.
scenes.beat: he is always on the crate now

prose: Klaus der Blitz: Listen. You need money faster than the day shift gives it to you. I've watched you do the sums on your hand.
Klaus der Blitz: There's a night route. Off the roster. Harbour to the industrial park, twenty-two hundred to four. Sixty euros, cash, no receipt.
Klaus der Blitz: The road out there has no lights and the potholes will try to kill you. I did it for six years. Look at me. Look at the leg.
Klaus der Blitz: I'm not recommending it. I'm telling you it exists, because somebody told me and I'd rather it was me that told you.

choices.label: Take the night route. Sixty euros is sixty euros.
"No. I've seen your knee."
prose: Klaus der Blitz is quiet for a second.
Klaus der Blitz: Good. Say it like that every time they offer. It gets harder to say every time.

scenes.beat: THE TEMPTATION: 60 euros against your own body

prose: Klaus der Blitz: Again?

choices.label: "Not tonight."
prose: Klaus der Blitz: Mm. Good.

scenes.beat: it gets harder to say no every time

prose: No lights past the harbour. The road surface goes from cobbles to concrete to something that is mostly holes with concrete between them.

prose.text: You make it. Sixty euros in your inside pocket, warm from your own body. You have never been this awake or this tired at the same time.
You know where the bad holes are now. You know because of what happened to your shoulder last time.
You catch yourself doing the sum on the ride home: how many more of these until two-fifty. That is exactly the sum Klaus was doing fourteen years ago.

prose: Wallet: {wallet}€. Body: {body}.
Something is wrong with your hands in the morning. They work, they just take a moment to agree to.

choices.label: Sleep, if you can call it that.

scenes.beat: FAST MONEY / logged against you in act_five

prose: Three in the morning. Nico is at the kitchen table with his laptop shut and his hands flat on top of it.

choices.label: "You're up."
prose: Nico: Yeah.

choices.label: Sit down without saying anything.
prose: You sit. He doesn't look up. After a while he starts talking anyway, which is what he needed.

scenes.beat: KNOT 4 / the 3am table

prose: Nico: Re-enrollment. Third year. It's a hundred and twenty euros and I have thirty-one.
Nico: If I miss it I'm not a student. If I'm not a student the visa goes. If the visa goes I go.
He says it very calmly, in order, like he has said it to himself many times in this chair.
Nico: Deadline's the nineteenth.

choices.label: Give him the hundred and twenty.
"Come to Kruma with me. Nina's short of people."
"I don't have it. I'm sorry. I really don't have it."

scenes.beat: THE ASK HE DOES NOT MAKE: 120 euros by the 19th

prose: You count it out on the table. It is most of what you have and all of your last eleven days.

Nico does not say thank you. He says, "I'll have it back to you by the ninth of next month," in a completely flat voice, and writes it on the back of his hand in biro, and that is somehow much bigger than thank you.
Wallet: {wallet}€.

choices.label: Go to bed. The two-fifty just got further away.
prose: You lie there and run the numbers and the numbers are worse.
You have never once been less sorry about numbers.

scenes.beat: THE REAL SACRIFICE: pushes tuition 11 days back

prose: You take him in at six. Nina looks him up and down for two seconds.
Nina Voss: Can you read?
Nico: I'm in my third year of law.
Nina Voss: So, no. Bottom shelf is der. Go.
He is bad at it. He is so much worse at it than you were, and watching that is the best feeling you have had in this country.
Nico, at the end of the shift, holding his back: How do you DO this every day.
scenes.beat: THE THIRD WAY: teach instead of pay

prose: Nico: No. Of course. I wasn't - I wasn't asking. I was just saying it out loud to somebody.
He opens the laptop again. The light goes blue on his face.
Nico: Go to bed. You've got a shift.

choices.label: Go to bed.
prose: You lie in Room 4 and listen to him not typing.

scenes.beat: COST OF SAYING NO / leads to the empty room on day 19

prose: Room 3 has the door open and nothing in it. Somebody has taken the poster down and left the tape.
Nico is asleep on the kitchen table with a highlighter still in his hand. You put the blanket from the sofa over him and take the highlighter, because he'll roll onto it.
scenes.beat: either you cover him with a blanket, or you look at tape

prose: Outside it is cold and completely bright.
You have {wallet}€, a body at {body}, a residence permit valid for three years, and a folder that cost eighty cents.
You walk back through the Marktplatz and you know the names of eleven people between here and the WG, and four of them wave.
Martha bangs on the bakery window with the flat of her hand and points at the oven, which means sit down, which means she has already put something on a plate.
You came here four weeks ago with twenty euros and it turns out that was never the number that mattered.
THE END - "Angekommen." Arrived.
You walk back through the Marktplatz. You made it. Every single number came out right and the folder is full and the stamp is real.
You pass the bakery and Martha is in the window and you nod, and she nods, and you keep walking because there is a shift at six.
You have the visa. Three years. You will work out the rest of it in the second one.
THE END - "Geschafft." Managed it.
You walk back through the Marktplatz and you cannot feel very much about it.
The stamp is real. The permit is three years. You beat every number and the numbers were the only thing you spoke to for two of those four weeks.
Klaus was on his crate for fourteen years and he was somebody's friend for none of them. You put the folder in your bag and you think about that all the way home.
Three years is a long time. Long enough to do it differently.
THE END - "Ueberlebt." Survived.
